resources.title: The Harvesters
resources.creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, 1565
resources.note: A great painting to practise slow looking — count how many different activities you can find.

resources.title: See Think Wonder
resources.note: A simple three-step way to explore any artwork, made for children and young people.

resources.title: Looking and Learning in the Art Museum, Lesson 1
resources.note: A lesson on describing and analyzing an artwork using the elements of art. Ages 11+.

title: How to Look at Art: See, Think, Wonder
summary: Looking closely is a skill. Slow down, describe what you see, say what it makes you think, then ask your own questions — every artwork opens up when you do.

keyConcepts: Art of the present and recent past
The idea can matter most (conceptual art)
Asking questions instead of giving answers
tryIt: Choose an everyday object. Write one sentence that turns it into an artwork — what is the idea? Give it a title and a museum label.

resources.title: Who is Yayoi Kusama?
resources.note: A kids' guide (with video) to the artist famous for dots and mirror rooms.

resources.title: Contemporary art (Art Term)
resources.note: What 'contemporary' means — and why museums disagree about when it begins.

resources.title: Conceptual art (Art Term)
resources.note: When the idea behind an artwork is more important than how it looks. Ages 11+.

title: What Is Contemporary Art?
summary: Contemporary art is art of our own time. Artists use anything — paint, light, mirrors, video, everyday objects — and often care more about the idea than the material.
imageNote: Most contemporary artworks are still protected by copyright, so this topic links to museum pages instead of showing pictures.

keyConcepts: Light and shadow through cut paper
tryIt: Fold a square of paper in half twice. Cut small shapes along the folds, then open it up. Shine a flashlight through it onto a wall.

resources.title: Silhouette of Eliza McPherson
resources.creator: W. Bruff, 19th century (hollow cut paper)
resources.note: A portrait made only from a cut-out outline — no drawing at all.

resources.title: Make a paper kaleidoscope
resources.note: Cut, fold and play with reflected color.

resources.title: Collage play
resources.note: Cut-and-paste ideas for building pictures from paper scraps.

title: Paper Cutting & Silhouettes
summary: With only paper and scissors you can make portraits, patterns and whole scenes. A silhouette shows just the outline — so the shape has to say everything.

keyConcepts: Changing an object by wrapping it
Planning with a quick sketch first
tryIt: Make a standing animal from one cereal box using only cuts and slots — no tape. Can it stand on its own?

resources.title: Wrap It Up
resources.note: Wrap everyday objects in fabric and string to turn them into new shapes.

resources.title: Make a hanging mobile
resources.note: A light, moving sculpture that catches the light.

resources.title: Make a paper pumpkin sculpture
resources.note: Fold and cut a paper pumpkin, then cover it in dots.

title: Build It: Sculpture from Everyday Materials
summary: Cardboard, paper, string and fabric can become sculpture. Artists build by folding, joining, stacking, hanging and even wrapping ordinary things.

keyConcepts: Score and slip to join pieces
Keep it chunky — thin parts break
tryIt: Make a small head from one ball of clay. Push, pinch and poke to make the features — no adding extra pieces.

resources.title: Head of a Male Haniwa Figure with Hat
resources.creator: Japan, Kofun period, ca. 6th century (earthenware)
resources.note: Simple holes for eyes and mouth — still full of personality, 1,500 years later.

resources.title: #MetKids—How Do We Make Art at The Met?
resources.note: Kids make tiles and clay sculptures inspired by the museum.

title: Clay: Shaping by Hand
summary: People have shaped clay for thousands of years — pinching, rolling coils and joining slabs. Simple forms can be full of character.

keyConcepts: Folding one sheet into eight pages
tryIt: Fold one sheet into a mini-zine about your favorite animal: cover, five facts, a drawing, and a back page.

resources.title: How to Make a Zine
resources.note: Step-by-step film with an artist and students. You need one sheet of paper, scissors and glue.

title: Make Your Own Book or Zine
summary: A zine is a small, home-made booklet. One sheet of paper can become an eight-page book full of drawings, collage and your own stories.

keyConcepts: Stop-motion: move it, photograph it, repeat
tryIt: Make a flipbook on a stack of sticky notes: draw a ball on the last page, then move it a little higher on each page above. Flip from the back!

resources.title: Animal Locomotion, Volume IX: Horses
resources.creator: Eadweard Muybridge, 1887 (photogravures)
resources.note: Muybridge photographed movement frame by frame — an early step toward film and animation.

resources.title: Be an Animator
resources.note: Model a clay character, plan a storyboard and make a stop-motion film with a tablet or phone.

resources.title: Pixar in a Box
resources.publisher: Khan Academy, with Pixar Animation Studios
resources.note: Free video lessons from Pixar artists, including storytelling and how animation works. Ages 10+.

title: How Animation Works: Frames and Motion
summary: Animation is a trick of the eye: many still pictures shown quickly look like movement. Even a few frames can make a ball bounce or a horse gallop.

tryIt: Draw a six-box storyboard of your morning, from waking up to leaving home. Use at least one close-up and one wide view.

resources.title: Pixar in a Box
resources.publisher: Khan Academy, with Pixar Animation Studios
resources.note: Free video lessons from Pixar artists, including storytelling and how animation works. Ages 10+.

resources.title: Be an Animator (storyboard step)
resources.note: Includes a storyboard sheet for planning your own short film.

title: Storyboards: Planning a Story in Pictures
summary: Before a film or comic is made, artists sketch it as a row of small boxes. A storyboard shows what happens, where the 'camera' is, and how the story flows.

keyConcepts: Same design rules: shape, color, composition
tryIt: Draw the same doodle three times, changing one small thing each time. Flip between them quickly — you've made a three-frame loop.

resources.title: Make a Doodle GIF
resources.note: Turn a few drawings into a looping animation.

resources.title: Draw a Sound Creature
resources.note: Let sounds guide the shapes you draw.

resources.title: Make a Drawing Robot
resources.note: Build a simple wobbling machine that makes its own marks.

title: Digital Drawing and Creative Technology
summary: Screens, code and sound can all be art tools. Digital artists experiment with GIFs, drawing machines and interactive pictures.
imageNote: Most digital artworks are recent and protected by copyright, so this topic links to activities instead of showing pictures.

keyConcepts: Symbols from nature (the Nile, plants, animals)
Rules that lasted thousands of years
tryIt: Design a small animal 'helper' for a journey. Decorate it with symbols of where it lives, the way the hippo's body is covered with river plants.

resources.title: Hippopotamus ("William")
resources.creator: Egypt, Middle Kingdom, ca. 1961–1878 B.C. (faience)
resources.note: Look closely: lotus flowers and river plants are painted on its body — it carries its home with it.

resources.title: How William the Hippo Got His Name
resources.creator: Isabel Stünkel and Kei Yamamoto
resources.note: The story of the museum's favorite hippo and how it got its nickname. Ages 10+.

title: Ancient Egypt: Art Made to Last Forever
summary: Egyptian artists made objects for the afterlife, so they used strong, simple shapes and lasting materials. Even a small blue hippo could carry big meaning.

tryIt: Draw a figure in front of a window that shows a landscape. Make the faraway hills smaller and paler than the figure.

resources.title: Madonna and Child
resources.creator: Filippino Lippi, ca. 1483–84
resources.note: Notice the open window and the deep landscape behind the figures — a Renaissance favorite.

resources.title: How one-point linear perspective works
resources.creator: Dr. Beth Harris and Dr. Steven Zucker
resources.note: How Renaissance artists invented a system for painting deep space.

title: The Renaissance: A New Way of Seeing
summary: In 15th-century Italy, artists studied people, nature and space more closely than ever. Perspective and soft, believable light made paintings feel like windows.

tryIt: Paint or draw the same object in the morning and in the evening. What happened to the colors?

resources.title: Water Lilies
resources.creator: Claude Monet, 1906
resources.note: No horizon, no sky — just water, reflections and floating flowers.

resources.title: Impressionism: Art and Modernity
resources.creator: Margaret Samu
resources.note: How a group of painters broke the rules in 1874 and changed art. Ages 12+.

title: Impressionism: Painting Light and Moments
summary: The Impressionists painted quickly, often outdoors, to catch light as it changed. Loose brushstrokes and bright color showed a moment, not every detail.

keyConcepts: Brush and ink as the main tools
Landscape as a mirror of the mind
tryIt: Draw a landscape in a long, narrow strip. Put tiny travelers on a path, and leave misty empty spaces between the mountains.

resources.title: Old Trees, Level Distance
resources.creator: Guo Xi, China, Northern Song dynasty, ca. 1080 (handscroll, ink and color on silk)
resources.note: Follow the river from right to left, the way a handscroll is unrolled.

resources.title: Landscape Painting in Chinese Art
resources.creator: Department of Asian Art
resources.note: How landscape became the most important subject in Chinese painting. Ages 12+.

title: Chinese Landscape Painting: Mountains, Mist and Mind
summary: Chinese landscape painters didn't copy one view. They gathered memories of mountains, trees and water into a journey the viewer travels with their eyes.
